bibl.title: Defining Feasibility and Pilot Studies in Preparation for Randomised Controlled Trials: Development of a Conceptual Framework

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: TWO WORDS USED INTERCHANGEABLY BY THE RESEARCHERS WHO DEPEND ON THEM - `pilot` and `feasibility` for studies run before a definitive randomised trial - re-defined by a team that proposed mutually exclusive definitions and was overruled by its own panel
span.quote: We initially adopted mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies. However, some Delphi survey respondents and the majority of open meeting attendees disagreed with the idea of mutually exclusive definitions. Their viewpoint was supported by definitions outside the health research context, the use of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ in the literature, and participants at the international consensus meeting. In our framework, pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies, rather than the two being mutually exclusive. A feasibility study asks whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A pilot study asks the same questions but also has a specific design feature: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, is conducted on a smaller scale.

span.label: whether pilot and feasibility studies can be given mutually exclusive definitions consistent with how authors actually describe their studies
span.quote: Our third hypothesis, namely that it is not possible to apply unique mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies in preparation for an RCT that are consistent with the way authors describe their studies, is supported by the characteristics of studies presented in Table 1 and summarised in Table 2 . We could find no design or other features (such as randomisation or presence of a control group) that distinguished between those that investigators called feasibility studies and those that they called pilot studies.

span.label: a conceptual framework in which feasibility is the overarching concept and pilot studies are a subset of it, with three named types beneath, validated against 27 published studies and an international consensus meeting
span.quote: We reached consensus over a conceptual framework for the definitions of these studies in which feasibility is an overarching concept for studies assessing whether a future study, project or development can be done. For studies conducted in preparation for a RCT assessing the effect of a therapy or intervention, three distinct types of study come under the umbrella of feasibility studies: randomised pilot studies, non-randomised pilot studies, feasibility studies that are not pilot studies. Thus pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies.

span.label: method
span.quote: Within our framework we define all studies aiming to assess whether a future RCT is do-able as ‘feasibility studies’.

span.label: two national funders of the same research holding contradictory definitions in print, and 63% of published studies using both words for one study
span.quote: These various, sometimes conflicting, approaches to the interpretation of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ exemplify differences in current usage and opinion in the research community.

span.label: a two-round Delphi of 93 then 79 participants, an open meeting vote at a trials methodology conference, a review of definitions from OUTSIDE health research, a systematic review of 27 studies, and a 19-person international consensus meeting
span.term: a two-round Delphi of 93 then 79 participants, an open meeting vote at a trials methodology conference, a review of definitions from OUTSIDE health research, a systematic review of 27 studies, and a 19-person international consensus meeting
span.quote: There was a wide range of participants in the open meeting, including senior quantitative and qualitative methodologists, and a funding body representative. The four propositions we devised to cover different views about definitions of pilot and feasibility studies are shown in Fig 5 . Fourteen out of the fifteen attendees who voted on these propositions preferred propositions 3 or 4, based on comments from the Delphi survey and the MRC guidance on designing and evaluating complex interventions respectively. Neither of these propositions implied mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies.

span.label: **A RESEARCH TEAM PROPOSED A DEFINITION AND WAS VOTED DOWN BY ITS OWN PANEL, AND PUBLISHED THAT**: `We INITIALLY ADOPTED MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE DEFINITIONS of pilot and feasibility studies. HOWEVER, SOME DELPHI SURVEY RESPONDENTS AND THE MAJORITY OF OPEN MEETING ATTENDEES DISAGREED WITH THE IDEA OF MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE DEFINITIONS.` The corpus has committees that vote and panels that disagree. **This is the first where the definition on the table was the AUTHORS' OWN and the vote went against them**
span.quote: We initially adopted mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies. However, some Delphi survey respondents and the majority of open meeting attendees disagreed with the idea of mutually exclusive definitions. Their viewpoint was supported by definitions outside the health research context, the use of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ in the literature, and participants at the international consensus meeting. In our framework, pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies, rather than the two being mutually exclusive. A feasibility study asks whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A pilot study asks the same questions but also has a specific design feature: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, is conducted on a smaller scale.

span.label: AND THE VOTE IS REPORTED WITH ITS MARGIN: `FOURTEEN OUT OF THE FIFTEEN ATTENDEES who voted on these propositions PREFERRED PROPOSITIONS 3 OR 4, based on comments from the Delphi survey and the MRC guidance ... NEITHER OF THESE PROPOSITIONS IMPLIED MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE DEFINITIONS.` Four propositions were put; the two that survived both contradicted the team's starting position
span.quote: There was a wide range of participants in the open meeting, including senior quantitative and qualitative methodologists, and a funding body representative. The four propositions we devised to cover different views about definitions of pilot and feasibility studies are shown in Fig 5 . Fourteen out of the fifteen attendees who voted on these propositions preferred propositions 3 or 4, based on comments from the Delphi survey and the MRC guidance on designing and evaluating complex interventions respectively. Neither of these propositions implied mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies.

span.label: **AND 70% APPROVAL WAS TREATED AS A FAILING SCORE, BECAUSE IT WAS THE LOWEST IN THE INSTRUMENT**: `OVER 70% of participants in the first round FELT THAT OUR DEFINITIONS ... WERE APPROPRIATE. HOWEVER, THESE FOUR ITEMS HAD SOME OF THE LOWEST APPROPRIATENESS RATINGS IN THE SURVEY and there were a large number of comments.` bishop2017 took 78% against a declared 75% target as adequate. **Eldridge read the RANK and Bishop read the THRESHOLD, on the same kind of number, in the same method** - and neither reading is wrong, which is the point
span.quote: Over 70% of participants in the first round felt that our definitions, the way we had distinguished between pilot and feasibility studies, and the labels ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ were appropriate. However, these four items had some of the lowest appropriateness ratings in the survey and there were a large number of comments

span.label: AND THE REPLACEMENT IS SUBSUMPTION, WITH THE DIFFERENTIA A DESIGN FEATURE RATHER THAN A QUESTION: `A FEASIBILITY STUDY ASKS whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A PILOT STUDY ASKS THE SAME QUESTIONS BUT ALSO HAS A SPECIFIC DESIGN FEATURE: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, IS CONDUCTED ON A SMALLER SCALE.` **The two classes share their entire question set and differ only in method** - so the corollary is that `ALL PILOT STUDIES ARE FEASIBILITY STUDIES BUT NOT ALL FEASIBILITY STUDIES ARE PILOT STUDIES`
span.quote: We therefore agreed that a pilot study is a study in which a future study or part of a future study , is conducted on a smaller scale to ask the question whether something can be done , should we proceed with it , and if so , how . The corollary of these definitions is that all pilot studies are feasibility studies but not all feasibility studies are pilot studies.

span.label: **AND TWO NATIONAL FUNDERS OF THE SAME RESEARCH DISAGREE IN PRINT**: NIHR has `a SMALLER VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together`, and `NEVERTHELESS, IT STILL CONTRASTS WITH THE MRC FRAMEWORK GUIDANCE that explicitly states: `A PILOT STUDY NEED NOT BE A `SCALE MODEL` of the planned main-stage evaluation, but should address the main uncertainties`.` Both live, both authoritative, and a grant application must satisfy one of them
span.quote: The NIHR wording for pilot studies has been changed more recently to ‘a smaller version of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’ ( Fig 1 ). Nevertheless, it still contrasts with the MRC framework guidance that explicitly states: ‘A pilot study need not be a “scale model” of the planned main-stage evaluation, but should address the main uncertainties that have been identified in the development work’ [ 2 ].

span.label: **AND THE CLASS THE FRAMEWORK MOST NEEDS RETURNED ZERO, BECAUSE OF A NAMING PRACTICE**: `our electronic search WAS UNABLE TO IDENTIFY ANY FEASIBILITY STUDIES THAT WERE NOT PILOT STUDIES according to our definitions. Subsequent discussion with qualitative researchers suggested that this is because SUCH STUDIES ARE OFTEN NOT DESCRIBED AS FEASIBILITY STUDIES IN THE TITLE OR ABSTRACT.` A zero that names only its own shape - **and they knew the class existed because they had two specimens before they built the search**
span.quote: Lastly, our electronic search was unable to identify any feasibility studies that were not pilot studies according to our definitions. Subsequent discussion with qualitative researchers suggested that this is because such studies are often not described as feasibility studies in the title or abstract.

span.label: AND THE FAILED HYPOTHESIS IS REPORTED WITH THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE THE AUTHORS ALREADY HELD: `the fourth hypothesis ... WAS NOT SUPPORTED; WE IDENTIFIED NO SUCH STUDIES amongst those reported in Table 1. NEVERTHELESS, WE HAD IDENTIFIED TWO PRIOR TO CARRYING OUT THE REVIEW.` A negative result published beside the two cases that contradict it
span.quote: However, the fourth hypothesis, that amongst studies in preparation for an RCT evaluating the effect of an intervention or therapy it is possible to identify some studies that explore the feasibility of a certain intervention or acquire related information about the feasibility of applying an intervention in a future study but are not pilot studies, was not supported; we identified no such studies amongst those reported in Table 1 . Nevertheless, we had identified two prior to carrying out the review [ 10 , 15 ].

span.label: AND NO DESIGN FEATURE SEPARATES THE TWO IN PRACTICE: `WE COULD FIND NO DESIGN OR OTHER FEATURES (such as randomisation or presence of a control group) THAT DISTINGUISHED BETWEEN THOSE THAT INVESTIGATORS CALLED FEASIBILITY STUDIES AND THOSE THAT THEY CALLED PILOT STUDIES.` The word is not tracking anything in the study - it is tracking the author
span.quote: Our third hypothesis, namely that it is not possible to apply unique mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies in preparation for an RCT that are consistent with the way authors describe their studies, is supported by the characteristics of studies presented in Table 1 and summarised in Table 2 . We could find no design or other features (such as randomisation or presence of a control group) that distinguished between those that investigators called feasibility studies and those that they called pilot studies.

span.label: AND THE WORKED CASE IS THREE PAPERS WITH ONE DESIGN AND THREE LABELS: `Lee et al, Boogerd et al and Wolf et al ALL DESCRIBE RANDOMISED STUDIES EXPLORING THE FEASIBILITY OF INTRODUCING NEW SYSTEMS ... but Lee et al describe their study as `A RANDOMIZED CONTROL PILOT STUDY`, with the word `feasibility` used in the abstract and text, while the study by Boogerd et al is titled `TEAMING UP: FEASIBILITY OF AN ONLINE TREATMENT ENVIRONMENT`, and Wolf at al describe their study AS A PILOT STUDY WITHOUT USING THE WORD `FEASIBILITY`.` Same shape, three vocabularies
span.quote: For example Lee et al [ 31 ], Boogerd et al [ 22 ] and Wolf et al [ 38 ] all describe randomised studies exploring the feasibility of introducing new systems (brain computer interface memory training game, on-line interactive treatment environment, bed-exit alarm respectively) but Lee et al describe their study as a ‘A Randomized Control Pilot Study’, with the word ‘feasibility’ used in the abstract and text, while the study by Boogerd et al . is titled ‘Teaming up: feasibility of an online treatment environment for adolescents with type 1 diabetes’, and Wolf at al describe their study as a pilot study without using the word ‘feasibility’.

span.label: AND THE DEFINITIONS WERE ANCHORED DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE THE FIELD: `Definitions of feasibility OUTSIDE THE HEALTH RESEARCH CONTEXT focus on the likelihood of being able to do something. For example, THE OXFORD ON-LINE DICTIONARY defines feasibility as: `The state or degree of being easily or conveniently done` ... `THE FEASIBILITY STUDY IS AN EVALUATION AND ANALYSIS OF THE POTENTIAL OF A PROPOSED PROJECT`.` A technical vocabulary corrected against ordinary usage, on purpose, and the panel's own viewpoint `WAS SUPPORTED BY DEFINITIONS OUTSIDE THE HEALTH RESEARCH CONTEXT`
span.quote: Definitions of feasibility outside the health research context focus on the likelihood of being able to do something. For example, the Oxford on-line dictionary defines feasibility as: ‘The state or degree of being easily or conveniently done’ [ 14 ] and a feasibility study as: ‘An assessment of the practicality of a proposed plan or method’ [ 15 ]. Some definitions also suggest that a feasibility study should help with decision making, for example [ 16 ]: ‘The feasibility study is an evaluation and analysis of the potential of a proposed project. It is based on extensive investigation and research to support the process of decision making’.

span.label: AND THE WORD IS YOUNGER THAN THE FIELD: `the use of the word `PILOT` to mean something that is A PROTOTYPE of something else ONLY APPEARS TO EMERGE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE TWENTIETH CENTURY and the first use of the word in relation to research design that we could find was IN 1947 - A PILOT SURVEY. Thus WE DO NOT HAVE TO LOOK VERY FAR BACK TO SEE CHANGES IN THE USE of one of the words.` A term whose sense is seventy years old being repaired by a committee
span.quote: In fact, the use of the word ‘pilot’ to mean something that is a prototype of something else only appears to emerge in the middle of the twentieth century and the first use of the word in relation to research design that we could find was in 1947—a pilot survey [ 58 ]. Thus we do not have to look very far back to see changes in the use of one of the words we have been dealing with in developing our conceptual framework.

span.label: AND A COMPETING FRAMEWORK IS NAMED AND REFUSED: `Bugge et al in developing THE ADEPT FRAMEWORK refer to the NIHR definitions ... ALTHOUGH NOT EXPLICITLY STATED, THE TEXT SEEMS TO SUGGEST THAT PILOT AND FEASIBILITY STUDIES ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE. OUR WORK INDICATES THAT THIS IS NEITHER NECESSARY NOR DESIRABLE.` The rejected position is read out of a text that never states it - an inference about somebody else's definition, marked as an inference
span.quote: For example, Bugge et al in developing the ADEPT framework refer to the NIHR definitions and suggest that feasibility studies ask questions about ‘whether the study can be done’ while pilot trials are ‘(a miniature version of the main trial), which aim to test aspects of study design and processes for the implementation of a larger main trial in the future’ [ 49 ]. Although not explicitly stated, the text seems to suggest that pilot and feasibility studies are mutually exclusive. Our work indicates that this is neither necessary nor desirable.

span.label: A PAPER WHOSE STATED MOTIVATION IS TERMINOLOGICAL INCONSISTENCY: `ONE MOTIVATING FACTOR FOR THE WORK REPORTED IN THIS PAPER WAS THE INCONSISTENT USE OF TERMS.` Not a limitation, not an aside - the reason the work was done, in the paper's own words.
span.quote: One motivating factor for the work reported in this paper was the inconsistent use of terms. For example, in the context of RCTs ‘pilot study’ is sometimes

span.label: A DEFINITION REVISED BY ONE WORD, AND THE PAPER DATES IT: `The NIHR wording for pilot studies HAS BEEN CHANGED MORE RECENTLY to ‘A SMALLER VERSION of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’.` `A version` became `a smaller version`. The scale-model implication was already the contested part, and the revision sharpens rather than removes it.
span.quote: The NIHR wording for pilot studies has been changed more recently to ‘a smaller version of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’ ( Fig 1 )

span.label: AND ANOTHER FUNDER'S GUIDANCE CONTRADICTS IT IN TERMS: `Nevertheless, it STILL CONTRASTS WITH THE MRC FRAMEWORK GUIDANCE THAT EXPLICITLY STATES: ‘A PILOT STUDY NEED NOT BE A “SCALE MODEL” [of the planned main-stage evaluation]’.` Two national research funders publishing definitions of the same term that deny each other, and a third document reporting both.
span.quote: Nevertheless, it still contrasts with the MRC framework guidance that explicitly states: ‘A pilot study need not be a “scale model”

span.label: AND SOMEBODY TESTED WHICH DEFINITION THE LITERATURE ACTUALLY FOLLOWS - IN 2010, AND THE RECORD IS IN THIS CORPUS: `ARAIN ET AL. FELT THAT THE NIHR DEFINITIONS WERE HELPFUL, AND SHOWED THAT STUDIES IDENTIFIED USING THE KEYWORD ‘FEASIBILITY’ HAD DIFFERENT CHARACTERISTICS FROM THOSE IDENTIFIED AS ‘PILOT’ STUDIES.` That is an empirical test of whether two labels pick out different things, run on the labels themselves - the method this project uses, applied by a paper we hold (`arain2010`) and cited by another we hold.
span.quote: Arain et al . felt that the NIHR definitions were helpful, and showed that studies identified using the keyword ‘feasibility’ had different characteristics from those identified as ‘pilot’ studies

span.label: **THEIR SCREENING INSTRUMENT MISSED SIX OF TEN, AND THEY MEASURED IT**: `Out of our exploratory sample of 30 study reports for which we reviewed FULL TEXTS rather than only titles and abstracts, we identified 10 that could be classed as pilot or feasibility studies using our framework. We had already identified four of these ... BUT HAD FAILED TO IDENTIFY THE OTHER SIX ... because key information ... WERE NOT INCLUDED IN THE ABSTRACT.` A deliberate false-negative rate for their own search, run and reported rather than assumed
span.quote: Out of our exploratory sample of 30 study reports for which we reviewed full texts rather than only titles and abstracts, we identified 10 that could be classed as pilot or feasibility studies using our framework. We had already identified four of these in our sample reported in Table 1 , but had failed to identify the other six. As expected, this was because key information to identify them as pilot or feasiblity studies such as the fact that they were in preparation for a larger RCT, or that the main objectives were to do with feasiblity were not included in the abstract. Thus our assumption that an initial screen using only abstracts resulted in the omission of some pilot and feasiblity studies was correct.

span.label: AND FEASIBILITY IS TREATED AS AN UMBRELLA THAT OTHER FRAMEWORKS SPLIT: `in other frameworks, such as THE RE-AIM FRAMEWORK, FEASIBILITY AND ACCEPTABILITY ARE SEEN AS TWO DIFFERENT CONCEPTS. However, IT IS PERFECTLY POSSIBLE TO EXPLORE THE ACCEPTABILITY of an intervention ... IN ORDER TO DETERMINE THE FEASIBILITY of a putative larger RCT.` The framework absorbs a distinction another framework maintains, and argues rather than measures the point
span.quote: Some might argue that the focus of their study in preparation for a future RCT is acceptability rather than feasibility, and indeed, in other frameworks, such as the RE-AIM framework [ 53 ], feasibility and acceptability are seen as two different concepts. However, it is perfectly possible to explore the acceptability of an intervention, of a data collection process or of randomisation in order to determine the feasibility of a putative larger RCT.

span.label: AND THE BOUNDARY IS DRAWN BY EXCLUSION AS WELL: `Within our framework, some important studies conducted in advance of a future RCT ... ARE NOT FEASIBILITY STUDIES. For example, A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW, usually an essential pre-requisite for such an RCT, NORMALLY ADDRESSES WHETHER THE FUTURE RCT IS NECESSARY OR DESIRABLE, NOT WHETHER IT IS FEASIBLE.` The class is bounded by the QUESTION ASKED, not by the work done - which is why a systematic review falls outside it
span.quote: Within our framework, some important studies conducted in advance of a future RCT to evaluate the effect of a therapy or intervention are not feasibility studies. For example, a systematic review, usually an essential pre-requisite for such an RCT, normally addresses whether the future RCT is necessary or desirable , not whether it is feasible .

span.label: AND THE PREDECESSOR DEFINITION IT REPLACES IS QUOTED: `Thabane et al also considered the relationship between pilot and feasibility, suggesting that FEASIBILITY SHOULD BE THE MAIN EMPHASIS OF A PILOT STUDY and that `A PILOT STUDY IS SYNONYMOUS WITH A FEASIBILITY STUDY intended to guide the planning of a large scale investigation`.` Synonymy in 2010, subsumption in 2016 - and the 2016 framework says the two are neither synonyms nor exclusive
span.quote: Thabane et al also considered the relationship between pilot and feasibility, suggesting that feasibility should be the main emphasis of a pilot study and that ‘a pilot study is synonymous with a feasibility study intended to guide the planning of a large scale investigation’.

span.label: reviewing the full texts of a random sample of 30 studies whose abstracts had already been screened, to measure what abstract-only screening missed
span.note: eliminates: an unmeasured false-negative rate in the paper's own search · outcome: failed
span.quote: Out of our exploratory sample of 30 study reports for which we reviewed full texts rather than only titles and abstracts, we identified 10 that could be classed as pilot or feasibility studies using our framework. We had already identified four of these in our sample reported in Table 1 , but had failed to identify the other six. As expected, this was because key information to identify them as pilot or feasiblity studies such as the fact that they were in preparation for a larger RCT, or that the main objectives were to do with feasiblity were not included in the abstract. Thus our assumption that an initial screen using only abstracts resulted in the omission of some pilot and feasiblity studies was correct.

span.label: taking the framework to a 19-person international consensus meeting that included the authors of the NIHR definitions and the MRC guidance being disagreed with
span.note: eliminates: a framework agreed only among people who already shared the authors' view · outcome: held
span.quote: There was a wide range of participants in the open meeting, including senior quantitative and qualitative methodologists, and a funding body representative. The four propositions we devised to cover different views about definitions of pilot and feasibility studies are shown in Fig 5 . Fourteen out of the fifteen attendees who voted on these propositions preferred propositions 3 or 4, based on comments from the Delphi survey and the MRC guidance on designing and evaluating complex interventions respectively. Neither of these propositions implied mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies.

span.label: checking the proposed definitions against definitions of `pilot` and `feasibility` from OUTSIDE health research - dictionaries and general project management
span.note: eliminates: a technical sense drifting away from the ordinary word it borrows · outcome: held
span.quote: Definitions of feasibility outside the health research context focus on the likelihood of being able to do something. For example, the Oxford on-line dictionary defines feasibility as: ‘The state or degree of being easily or conveniently done’ [ 14 ] and a feasibility study as: ‘An assessment of the practicality of a proposed plan or method’ [ 15 ]. Some definitions also suggest that a feasibility study should help with decision making, for example [ 16 ]: ‘The feasibility study is an evaluation and analysis of the potential of a proposed project. It is based on extensive investigation and research to support the process of decision making’.

span.label: pilot studies
span.quote: We initially adopted mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies. However, some Delphi survey respondents and the majority of open meeting attendees disagreed with the idea of mutually exclusive definitions. Their viewpoint was supported by definitions outside the health research context, the use of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ in the literature, and participants at the international consensus meeting. In our framework, pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies, rather than the two being mutually exclusive. A feasibility study asks whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A pilot study asks the same questions but also has a specific design feature: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, is conducted on a smaller scale.

span.quote: We initially adopted mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies. However, some Delphi survey respondents and the majority of open meeting attendees disagreed with the idea of mutually exclusive definitions. Their viewpoint was supported by definitions outside the health research context, the use of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ in the literature, and participants at the international consensus meeting. In our framework, pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies, rather than the two being mutually exclusive. A feasibility study asks whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A pilot study asks the same questions but also has a specific design feature: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, is conducted on a smaller scale.

span.label: studies aiming to assess whether a future RCT is do-able
span.term: studies aiming to assess whether a future RCT is do-able
span.quote: Within our framework we define all studies aiming to assess whether a future RCT is do-able as ‘feasibility studies’.

span.label: NIHR
span.quote: The NIHR wording for pilot studies has been changed more recently to ‘a smaller version of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’ ( Fig 1 ). Nevertheless, it still contrasts with the MRC framework guidance that explicitly states: ‘A pilot study need not be a “scale model” of the planned main-stage evaluation, but should address the main uncertainties that have been identified in the development work’ [ 2 ].

span.quote: The NIHR wording for pilot studies has been changed more recently to ‘a smaller version of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’ ( Fig 1 ). Nevertheless, it still contrasts with the MRC framework guidance that explicitly states: ‘A pilot study need not be a “scale model” of the planned main-stage evaluation, but should address the main uncertainties that have been identified in the development work’ [ 2 ].

span.label: feasibility
span.quote: Some might argue that the focus of their study in preparation for a future RCT is acceptability rather than feasibility, and indeed, in other frameworks, such as the RE-AIM framework [ 53 ], feasibility and acceptability are seen as two different concepts. However, it is perfectly possible to explore the acceptability of an intervention, of a data collection process or of randomisation in order to determine the feasibility of a putative larger RCT.

span.quote: Some might argue that the focus of their study in preparation for a future RCT is acceptability rather than feasibility, and indeed, in other frameworks, such as the RE-AIM framework [ 53 ], feasibility and acceptability are seen as two different concepts. However, it is perfectly possible to explore the acceptability of an intervention, of a data collection process or of randomisation in order to determine the feasibility of a putative larger RCT.

span.label: systematic review
span.quote: Within our framework, some important studies conducted in advance of a future RCT to evaluate the effect of a therapy or intervention are not feasibility studies. For example, a systematic review, usually an essential pre-requisite for such an RCT, normally addresses whether the future RCT is necessary or desirable , not whether it is feasible .

span.label: `feasibility study` (this framework) - `ALL STUDIES AIMING TO ASSESS WHETHER A FUTURE RCT IS DO-ABLE`; asks whether something can be done, should we proceed, and if so how
span.quote: Within our framework we define all studies aiming to assess whether a future RCT is do-able as ‘feasibility studies’.

span.label: `pilot study` (this framework) - the same questions PLUS a design feature: a future study or part of one is conducted ON A SMALLER SCALE. A subset of feasibility studies, not its complement
span.quote: We therefore agreed that a pilot study is a study in which a future study or part of a future study , is conducted on a smaller scale to ask the question whether something can be done , should we proceed with it , and if so , how . The corollary of these definitions is that all pilot studies are feasibility studies but not all feasibility studies are pilot studies.

span.label: `pilot study` (NIHR) - `a SMALLER VERSION OF THE MAIN STUDY used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together`; contrasted in the same paragraph with MRC's `NEED NOT BE A SCALE MODEL`
span.quote: The NIHR wording for pilot studies has been changed more recently to ‘a smaller version of the main study used to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’ ( Fig 1 ). Nevertheless, it still contrasts with the MRC framework guidance that explicitly states: ‘A pilot study need not be a “scale model” of the planned main-stage evaluation, but should address the main uncertainties that have been identified in the development work’ [ 2 ].

span.label: `pilot study` (Thabane 2010) - `SYNONYMOUS WITH a feasibility study intended to guide the planning of a large scale investigation`, the position this framework replaces
span.quote: Thabane et al also considered the relationship between pilot and feasibility, suggesting that feasibility should be the main emphasis of a pilot study and that ‘a pilot study is synonymous with a feasibility study intended to guide the planning of a large scale investigation’.

span.label: `pilot study` / `feasibility study` - SYNONYMOUS TO ONE BODY AND MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE TO ANOTHER, AT THE SAME TIME. Thabane (2010): `a pilot study is SYNONYMOUS WITH a feasibility study`. NIHR, `at about the same time`: definitions `THAT ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE`, with feasibility earlier in the process and a pilot `a version of the main study that is RUN IN MINIATURE`. The same two terms, the same years, opposite relations.
span.quote: However, at about the same time, the UK National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) developed definitions of pilot and feasibility studies that are mutually exclusive, suggesting that feasibility studies occurred slightly earlier in the research process and that pilot studies are ‘a version of the main study that is run in miniature to test whether the components of the main study can all work together’

span.label: extends → arain2010 - the review of current practice and editorial policy by an overlapping team, which showed that studies keyworded `feasibility` had different characteristics from those called `pilot`; this paper is the framework that follows it
span.quote: These various, sometimes conflicting, approaches to the interpretation of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ exemplify differences in current usage and opinion in the research community.

span.label: critiques → the ADEPT framework of Bugge et al, whose text `SEEMS TO SUGGEST THAT PILOT AND FEASIBILITY STUDIES ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE` - `NEITHER NECESSARY NOR DESIRABLE`
span.quote: For example, Bugge et al in developing the ADEPT framework refer to the NIHR definitions and suggest that feasibility studies ask questions about ‘whether the study can be done’ while pilot trials are ‘(a miniature version of the main trial), which aim to test aspects of study design and processes for the implementation of a larger main trial in the future’ [ 49 ]. Although not explicitly stated, the text seems to suggest that pilot and feasibility studies are mutually exclusive. Our work indicates that this is neither necessary nor desirable.

span.label: critiques → Thabane et al's 2010 position that `A PILOT STUDY IS SYNONYMOUS WITH A FEASIBILITY STUDY`, replaced here by subsumption

span.quote: We initially adopted mutually exclusive definitions of pilot and feasibility studies. However, some Delphi survey respondents and the majority of open meeting attendees disagreed with the idea of mutually exclusive definitions. Their viewpoint was supported by definitions outside the health research context, the use of the terms ‘pilot’ and ‘feasibility’ in the literature, and participants at the international consensus meeting. In our framework, pilot studies are a subset of feasibility studies, rather than the two being mutually exclusive. A feasibility study asks whether something can be done, should we proceed with it, and if so, how. A pilot study asks the same questions but also has a specific design feature: in a pilot study a future study, or part of a future study, is conducted on a smaller scale.
